source_text: Scribens itaque ad Romanos eo iam tempore, quo Gentium coeperat esse permixtio atque ideo tam ex Iudaeis quam ex Gentibus complebantur Ecclesiae, tumultus populi utriusque componit inculcans, quoniam nec Gentes impietatem suam, qua mutaverant gloriam Dei in similitudine imaginis hominis et volucrum et quadrupedum et serpentium, legis possint ignoratione diluere, quae per vim rationis ingenitae, etsi non ritum cerimoniarum Iudaicarum, tamen Deum innotescentem operibus, substantiae vero profunditate secretum, potuerint ex his, ab eo quae sunt facta, cognoscere. Legis autem normam, quantum ad vitae probitatem respicit, proprius unicuique suggerebat affectus, videlicet ut nihil tale inferret proximo, quale perpeti noluisset; atque ideo profanitatem Gentium iure optimo argui posse convincit, etsi non per legem, per eam tamen iustitiam, quae condidit legem, et qua iudicante hi, qui sine lege peccaverunt, sine lege et peribunt. Iudaeos vero, quorum magis intererat, quia in despectum Gentium maxime tumescebant, honorem sibi de legis purificationibus vindicantes ac per hoc aestimantes non sibi ita ut Gentibus profuisse Christi gratiam peccata donantem, quandoquidem legis ea institutione vitassent, magna disputationum virtute confringit allegans eis tanto amplius per indulgentiam fuisse collatum, quanto post legis admonitionem sine ulla ignoratione peccassent; per quod approbat eos reos fuisse et vehementer potuisse damnari in iustitiae examine, apud quem qui in lege peccaverunt, per legem iudicabuntur: Non enim auditores legis iusti sunt apud Deum, sed factores legis iustificabuntur [n209] . Hoc ergo proposito per totum librum disputans tum superbiam reprimit Iudaeorum, tum excusationem vanitatis Gentibus demit, ut doceat aequaliter ambobus populis Christi profuisse medicinam.
pass_a_gloss: Writing therefore to the Romans at that time already in which a mixing of the Gentiles had begun to be and therefore the Churches were being filled as much from Jews as from Gentiles, he composes the tumults of each people, stamping in that neither can the Gentiles wash away their impiety, by which they had changed the glory of God into a likeness of an image of a human being and of birds and of four-footed things and of serpents, by an ignorance of the law, which through the force of an inborn reason, even if not the rite of Jewish ceremonies, nevertheless God becoming known by works, but secret by the profundity of substance, they could have known from those things which have been made by him. But a proper affect was suggesting to each one the norm of the law, as far as it looks toward the honesty of life, namely that he would infer nothing of such a kind upon a neighbor as he would have been unwilling to suffer; and therefore he convicts that the profanity of the Gentiles can with best right be accused, even if not through the law, nevertheless through that justice which founded the law, and by which judging those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law. But the Jews, whose it more concerned, because they were swelling especially in contempt of the Gentiles, claiming for themselves an honor from the purifications of the law and through this estimating that the grace of Christ giving sins had not so profited them as the Gentiles, seeing that they would have avoided them by the institution of the law, he breaks by a great virtue of disputations, alleging to them that so much more was conferred through indulgence, as after the warning of the law they had sinned without any ignorance; through which he approves that they were defendants and could vehemently have been damned in an examination of justice, with whom those who have sinned in the law will be judged through the law: For not the hearers of the law are just with God, but the doers of the law will be justified. Disputing therefore with this purpose through the whole book he now represses the pride of the Jews, now takes from the Gentiles an excuse of vanity, so that he may teach that the medicine of Christ equally helped both peoples.

pass_b_english: Writing to the Romans at the time when the Gentiles had begun to be brought in, and churches were therefore being filled with Jews and Gentiles alike, he calms the disturbances of both peoples. He insists that the Gentiles cannot wash away their impiety—their exchanging God’s glory for a likeness of the image of a human being, birds, four-footed animals, and reptiles (Romans 1:23)—by pleading ignorance of the law. Through their inborn power of reason they could know God from what he had made: God disclosed through his works, though hidden in the depth of his substance, even if they did not know the observance of Jewish ceremonies (Romans 1:20). Each person’s own feeling suggested the rule of the law insofar as it concerns upright living: namely, to inflict on a neighbor nothing of the kind he would be unwilling to suffer himself (compare Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31; Tobit 4:15). He thus proves that the Gentiles’ impiety can quite rightly be condemned, even if not through the law, then through the justice that established the law. By its judgment, those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law (Romans 2:12). The Jews, however, had even more at stake. They were especially swollen with contempt for the Gentiles, claiming honor for themselves from the law’s purifications. They therefore supposed that Christ’s sin-forgiving grace had not benefited them as it benefited the Gentiles, since they had avoided those sins through the law’s instruction. He shatters this claim with powerful arguments, maintaining that they received all the more through forgiveness precisely because, after the law’s warning, they sinned without any ignorance. By this he proves that they were guilty and could have been severely condemned at justice’s examination, where those who sinned under the law will be judged through the law (Romans 2:12): ‘For it is not hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but doers of the law who will be justified’ (Romans 2:13) (Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31; Tobit 4:15). Arguing with this purpose throughout the book, he both restrains the Jews’ pride and removes the Gentiles’ excuse for their folly, to teach that Christ’s medicine benefited both peoples equally.
